Context you may rely on but must not simply repeat: an independent referee has separately audited the mathematical claims C1-C5 in the note (core reduction preserving e and m; the maximal-deletion lemma; ordinal-sum factors of cores; completeness of maximal-insertion-plus-ordinal-sum generation; e(P) >= |P| for cores) and returned all five as proved, with no counterexample. Separately, the Executive ran a fixed-budget exact minimax check on the generated core sets (1,053 cores with e<=33 all sortable in 6; 4,829 with e<=54 all sortable in 7) with known-answer controls, and independently enumerated all unlabeled posets for n<=8 (validated class counts) finding exactly the same 593 core classes with e<=33 as the generator.

Your job is to review the COMMIT itself, not to redo the research:
1. Verify the note's claims are accurately stated and correctly scoped: does it overclaim anywhere (especially \"T(6)=33\", \"T(7)=54\", \"complete generator\", the Lebesgue/typo level), does it correctly state what remains open (the all-r Fibonacci statement and Lemma A), and is the \"why it matters / what it does not give\" paragraph honest?
2. Check the code implements what the note says: generation rules, proper ideals only, level cap, canonical deduplication (is the canonical relabelling actually isomorphism-invariant?), exact comparison-game decision (no incorrect pruning), and that nothing silently depends on files outside the commit.
3. Run `python3 -m unittest tests.test_core_threshold -v` and verify the four tests genuinely test what their names say; run `python3 scripts/core_threshold_census.py --E 33 --h 6` and `--E 54 --h 7` and check the reported counts/failures. Also check that a deliberately too-small budget reports failures (the test covers this; confirm independently).
4. Check repo conventions: docstring/status labelling per AGENTS.md (\"experiment\", \"paper proof\"), no Lean changes, no scope violation, and that the note is consistent with docs/research-plan.md and docs/problem.md terminology.
